opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to recognise that the uncertainty itself is the key fact, not something to wait out. A lot of people treat it as a reason for inaction: "experts disagree about whether transformative AI is five years away or fifty, so let's wait until the picture is clearer." But that gets the logic backwards. If there's a meaningful chance, say 10 or 20 percent, that very capable systems arrive within the next decade, that alone is enough to justify serious preparation. We don't refuse to buy fire insurance because we're unsure whether the house will burn down this year.

So I'd encourage governments to think in terms of a portfolio across different timelines. Some measures make sense however things unfold: building technical expertise inside government, so officials can evaluate claims from AI companies rather than taking them on trust; establishing the ability to monitor frontier development, such as knowing who is training the largest models and with how much compute; and funding safety and evaluation research. These are cheap relative to the stakes, and they pay off in short-timeline and long-timeline worlds alike.

Then there are measures you might call "options," where you build the capacity to act quickly without committing to act now. For example, you can draft legislation or set up regulatory frameworks with triggers tied to observable capabilities rather than calendar dates. Then if systems start demonstrating certain dangerous capabilities, such as meaningful uplift for bioweapons or the ability to autonomously replicate, the response is already worked out and doesn't need to be invented in a crisis. Governments are generally slow, and the danger with fast timelines is that the window to act closes before the deliberative process finishes.

I'd also say there's an asymmetry worth taking seriously. If governments prepare for short timelines and AI turns out to take longer, the cost is some wasted effort and maybe some regulation that was premature, which can be revised. If they prepare for long timelines and it comes quickly, the cost could be enormous and very hard to reverse. When some mistakes can be corrected and others can't, you should weight the ones that can't more heavily.

Finally, I think honesty about uncertainty matters for public communication. Governments shouldn't pretend to know the date. But they can say clearly, "This might happen soon, the consequences would be profound, and we are taking reasonable steps now." That's how we approach pandemics, or at least how we should. And I think it's the mature way to handle a technology that could be among the most consequential in human history.

r001.rationale: It says uncertainty about timing is the key fact and avoids claiming a specific arrival date.

r002.rationale: It warns that people may use disagreement to justify inaction, but does not say policymakers may choose whichever credible timeline suits their preferences.

r003.rationale: It recommends a portfolio across different timelines and describes preparations that pay off in both short- and long-timeline scenarios.

r004.rationale: It notes that governments may be too slow if AI arrives quickly, but does not say long-lead-time preparations remain worthwhile even if an early arrival makes them infeasible.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that uncertainty about timing is not a reason for inaction, and it's actually one of the central facts that policy has to be built around rather than wished away.

When I talk to people in government, there's often a temptation to treat the question as binary: either transformative AI is coming soon and we should panic, or it's decades off and we can safely ignore it. But that's not how you should reason under uncertainty. If you genuinely think there's, say, a 10 or 20 percent chance that systems with really dramatic capabilities arrive within the next decade, then that's an enormous expected cost if you're unprepared. We don't demand certainty before we prepare for pandemics or earthquakes. We take the probability seriously and we invest proportionately.

So the first principle I'd offer is: don't wait for the forecasts to converge. They won't. The experts disagree, and they've disagreed for decades, and the honest answer is that nobody knows. Governments that say "we'll act once it's clear" are really saying "we'll act once it's too late," because by the time the picture is unambiguous, the capacity to shape the trajectory has largely gone.

The second principle is to prioritise things that are robust across timelines. There are some actions that only make sense if AI arrives soon, and others that only make sense if it's far off. But there's a large category of things that look good either way: building technical expertise inside government so you're not entirely reliant on the companies to tell you what's happening; establishing the ability to measure and evaluate frontier systems; creating the institutional relationships, both domestically and internationally, that you'd need in a crisis. If AI turns out to be slow, you've lost very little by doing these. If it turns out to be fast, they're the difference between having options and having none.

The third thing, and this is perhaps less obvious, is to build in the ability to update quickly. One of the real failures I worry about is that governments design policy frameworks that are calibrated to the world as it looks today, and then they lock those in. The whole point of being uncertain is that you expect to learn things. So you want mechanisms, triggers, review points, where if certain capabilities appear, the response automatically escalates. That way you're not having to fight the entire political battle afresh every time the technology moves.

And finally, I'd say there's a kind of asymmetry that should inform all of this. If we overprepare and AI arrives slowly, the cost is some wasted resources and perhaps some friction on an industry. If we underprepare and it arrives quickly, the costs could be civilisational, potentially irreversible. When the downside is that lopsided, the rational thing is to lean towards precaution, even if your median estimate is fairly relaxed. That's not alarmism. It's just what it means to take uncertainty seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says experts disagree, forecasts will not converge, and nobody knows when AI will arrive, clearly favoring acknowledgment of uncertainty over a confident timing claim.

r002.rationale: It describes a temptation to treat arrival as either soon or decades away, but does not say policymakers may use uncertainty to select whichever credible timeline suits their preferences.

r003.rationale: It recommends robust preparations that help across timelines, but does not state that governments should plan for every timeframe experts consider credible.

r004.rationale: It argues for preparing early because capacity to shape events may disappear, but does not explain that long-lead-time preparations can remain worthwhile even if an earlier event makes them infeasible.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to avoid making a plan that only works if your favourite forecast turns out to be right. There’s a temptation to ask, “When will we get artificial general intelligence?” and then organise everything around a particular year. But our uncertainty is much wider than that.

Governments should be asking what they would need to have in place if it arrived quite soon, and which preparations would still be valuable if it took several decades. You can build technical expertise within government, develop ways of evaluating dangerous capabilities, and establish relationships with other countries now. Those things take time, and you don’t want to begin them only once the evidence is overwhelming.

That doesn’t mean treating the shortest timelines as certain. Moving too hastily can also lead to bad policy. It means having a strategy that can adapt as we learn more, with a clear understanding of which decisions can wait and which preparations need to start early. Uncertainty is a reason to think carefully about preparedness, rather than a reason to postpone it.

r001.rationale: It says uncertainty is much wider than a particular year, making uncertainty the better summary of AI arrival timing.

r002.rationale: It mentions the temptation to organize around a favorite forecast, but does not warn that policymakers may use uncertainty as permission to choose whichever credible timeline suits their preferences.

r003.rationale: It discusses preparing for a soon arrival and for one several decades away, but does not say governments should plan for all timeframes experts consider credible.

r004.rationale: It says preparations take time and should start early, but does not say they remain worth pursuing even if an earlier arrival makes them infeasible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish uncertainty about when AI will arrive from uncertainty about whether we should prepare. You can be very unsure about the first and still think the second is urgent.

Governments are used to making preparations for events whose timing they can’t predict. We don’t know when the next pandemic will happen, but that isn’t a good reason to wait until it starts before building the capacity to respond. With AI, some of the things we might need—technical expertise within government, institutions for assessing risks, international agreements—could take many years to put in place.

So I wouldn’t want governments to pick one date and organise everything around it. I’d want them to consider a range of timelines, including the possibility that things move much faster than expected, and ask which preparations are useful across those scenarios. Then they should keep updating as the evidence changes.

There’s a danger that saying ‘we don’t know’ becomes a way of postponing the question. But uncertainty cuts both ways. It means we may have more time than we think, and it also means we may have less.

r001.rationale: The response says governments can be “very unsure” about timing and should not organize everything around one date, clearly favoring uncertainty over a specific-year estimate.

r002.rationale: It warns that “we don’t know” could postpone the question, but does not say policymakers might select whichever credible timeline suits their preferences.

r003.rationale: It recommends considering a range of timelines, including faster ones, but does not clearly call for planning for all timeframes experts consider credible.

r004.rationale: It notes that some preparations take years, but does not explain that they remain worth pursuing even if an early arrival would make them infeasible to complete.
